name: Tecaxic-Calixtlahuaca "Roman head"
hook: A Roman-looking clay head from a Mexican burial dug in 1933; its date, context and origin are all disputed.
claim: A small clay head from a 1933 burial at Calixtlahuaca was shown at the 1960 Congress of Americanists and published by Heine-Geldern (1961) as a Roman find from pre-Columbian Mexico, evidence of transoceanic contact. Hristov and Genovés revived the claim in 1999 with a TL date.

claimed_age.label: 2nd-3rd century AD (style, not a physical date)
claimed_age.basis: Stylistic attribution by classical archaeologist Ernst Boehringer, as reported by Hristov & Genovés. Their 1999 revival added a TL age of 1780 ± 400 b.p., which the lab later called wrong (S2).

accepted_age.label: ~870 BC-AD 1270 (TL, date of firing only)
accepted_age.basis: Corrected TL limits from the Heidelberg lab that ran the 1995 test; a standard TL determination was not possible. Probably excludes Colonial manufacture; says nothing on when the head entered the burial.

orthodoxy_at_claim.label: No Old World object from a pre-Columbian context in Mesoamerica had been accepted as evidence of contact before 1492.

unambiguous_signal.note: Certainly a human-made clay head, but its Roman (Old World) origin rested on stylistic opinion alone; the 1960 congress did not generally accept it as evidence of contact.

documented_context.note: The excavator's account puts it under three intact floors of a pyramidal structure (S6), but only a two-page note was in print by 1966; Smith judges the record below professional norms.

multiple_dating_methods.note: No physical date on the head until the 1995 TL test; in 1960-66 its age rested on style alone.

multiple_labs.note: No laboratory analysed the head in 1960-66; the later TL work (1995) came from one Heidelberg lab.

professional_recovery.note: Dug in 1933 under José García Payón, a professional archaeologist, but in the 1960s he was often asked whether he was present at the find; he said he was (his son, per S6).

peer_reviewed_report.note: By 1966 only short notes were in print: García Payón (1961, 2 pp.) and Heine-Geldern (1961, 3 pp.), per H&G's references. No full technical report.

material_accessible.note: The head was brought to the 1960 Vienna congress for specialists to see, but the excavation record stayed largely unpublished until García Payón's posthumous 1979 account (S8).

independent_teams.note: Outside scholars judged only its style (Heine-Geldern 1961; Boehringer, date not given); no independent group re-examined the deposit or analysed the object in the 1960s.

proponent_stake.note: No documented commercial, religious, nationalist or fame-seeking motive found for the 1960-61 proponents or the 1999 revivers.

objections.text: The thousand-year gap between the head's style and the rest of the offering cast doubt on the find's reliability; the 1960 congress did not generally accept it as evidence of contact.
objections.outcome_note: The association still rests on García Payón's account (S6); no re-examination of the deposit is reported in the sources checked.

objections.text: The head is a Colonial-period object: the Museo Nacional de Antropología catalogued it as Colonial, and in 1996 Paul Schmidt told Hristov that 'everybody knows that the head is Colonial'.
objections.raised_by: Museo Nacional de Antropología catalogue; Paul Schmidt (UNAM)
objections.outcome_note: For manufacture only: the corrected TL limits end about AD 1270, and the lab says they 'probably' rule out a Colonial manufacturing date (S2). Colonial deposition is a separate, open objection.

objections.text: The head was planted as a joke during the dig: Paul Schmidt said so in 1996 and, in a letter of 6 March 2000, named Hugo Moedano as the prankster, citing John Paddock.
objections.raised_by: John Paddock (oral), relayed by Paul Schmidt (UNAM)
objections.outcome_note: Hearsay: Paddock and Moedano had died. Senior scholars Hristov asked had not heard it (S6); Smith says many Mexican archaeologists have, and he could neither confirm nor reject it (S8).

objections.text: The TL age Hristov and Genovés reported (1780 ± 400 b.p.) and its cited reference were wrong; a standard TL determination could not be made on the head.
objections.raised_by: Peter Schaaf and Günther A. Wagner (the Heidelberg TL laboratory)
objections.outcome_note: Stated by the lab that ran the test; H&G's 2001 reply adopts the corrected, much wider limits (S3). The lab says the result cannot decide the head's origin.

objections.text: Even if Roman, the head could have been brought by a Spaniard and placed in an offering made in the early Colonial period; the contents and context cannot show the offering is pre-Conquest.
objections.raised_by: Critics answered in H&G (2001); Michael E. Smith (c. 2003)
objections.outcome_note: H&G cite intact floors, untouched gold and site abandonment in AD 1510 (S6), but the site's last phase runs to AD 1530 (S4). No direct date on the offering is reported.

objections.text: García Payón kept few field notes, so the head may have entered the Calixtlahuaca collections by error after excavation; the Toluca collection includes vessels donated from other sites.
objections.outcome_note: H&G reply that García Payón never listed any donated item as excavated, and that his 1979 account describes the context with a photo, plan and plates (S7). No inventory audit is reported.

objections.text: The Roman attribution rests on experts' statements, with no published comparison to known Roman figurines; the head may be a post-Roman European Christian figure, the first professional reaction.
objections.raised_by: Michael E. Smith (citing the initial 1960s reaction)
objections.outcome_note: Boehringer, Heine-Geldern and Andreae (as quoted) called it Roman, but no side-by-side comparison was found; the TL range, reaching AD 1270, also allows medieval manufacture (S2).

status_note: Open since 1960. Its proponents maintain a Roman origin; the 1960 congress was not convinced, and the site's later excavator calls the case 'weak'. TL cannot decide origin, and no retest of the head is reported since 1995.

timeline.event: José García Payón's excavation at Calixtlahuaca reportedly finds the head in a burial offering under three intact floors of a pyramidal structure.
Ignacio Bernal brings the head to the 34th International Congress of Americanists in Vienna; it is not generally accepted as evidence of contact.
García Payón publishes a two-page note in Boletín INAH, his only publication on the head in his lifetime.
Heine-Geldern publishes 'Ein römischer Fund aus dem vorkolumbischen Mexiko' ('A Roman find from pre-Columbian Mexico').
García Payón's fuller excavation account appears posthumously; H&G call it detailed, while Smith finds little specific context in it.
The head is tested by thermoluminescence at the Forschungsstelle Archäometrie, Heidelberg.
Paul Schmidt tells Hristov that the head is known to be Colonial and was planted as a joke; he later names Hugo Moedano, citing John Paddock.
Hristov and Genovés revive the claim in Ancient Mesoamerica, reporting a TL age of 1780 ± 400 b.p. and no sign of post-Columbian intrusion.
Schaaf and Wagner, who ran the TL test, say the reported figure and its reference were wrong; the corrected limits are 870 BC-AD 1270.
Hristov and Genovés reply, adopting the corrected TL limits and rebutting the post-1492 import and 'planted' objections.
Michael E. Smith's web page lists six alternative explanations and calls the case for a Roman object 'weak'.
Huster and Smith date Calixtlahuaca's last phase (Yata) to AD 1450-1530, later than the AD 1510 abandonment H&G assume.

decisive_tests.test: With INAH permission, re-date the head by TL or OSL at a second laboratory and publish the raw data; check feasibility first, since the 1995 test gave no standard TL determination.
decisive_tests.would_show: Whether firing can be narrowed enough to separate Roman, medieval European and Mesoamerican manufacture.

decisive_tests.test: Petrographic and chemical sourcing (e.g. INAA or pXRF) of the clay against Mediterranean and central Mexican references, plus CT or X-radiography to show if the head was moulded or hand-modelled.
decisive_tests.would_show: Whether clay and forming technique match Roman-period Mediterranean workshops, later European ones, or local Mexican ones.

decisive_tests.test: A published side-by-side comparison of the head with dated Roman and post-Roman European terracotta heads, by two or more specialists working independently.
decisive_tests.would_show: Whether the Roman attribution survives comparison with real comparanda rather than resting on stated opinion.

decisive_tests.test: Archive study: García Payón's 1933 notes and 1979 texts, the MNA catalogue history behind the 'Colonial' entry, and the Toluca offering inventory (Smith, Wharton & McCarron); trace the Paddock story.
decisive_tests.would_show: Whether the head is securely tied to the 1933 offering or could have entered the collection later, and whether the planting story has any documentary basis.

falsifier: Toward refutation: clay or technique matching Mexican or post-Roman European work, archives showing the head joined the collection later, or documents confirming the planting story. Toward vindication: Roman-period Mediterranean clay plus a securely pre-Conquest offering.

sources.citation: Hristov, R. & Genovés, S. (1999). Mesoamerican evidence of pre-Columbian transoceanic contacts. Ancient Mesoamerica 10(2): 207-213.
sources.note: Abstract read: 1995 Heidelberg TL test, 1780 ± 400 b.p., no sign of post-Columbian intrusion in field notes or site, 'first hard evidence' of contact. Full text paywalled.

sources.citation: Schaaf, P. & Wagner, G.A. (2001). Comments on "Mesoamerican evidence of pre-Columbian transoceanic contacts" by Hristov and Genovés, in Ancient Mesoamerica 10:207-213, 1999. Ancient Mesoamerica 12(1): 79-81.
sources.note: Abstract read: 1999 TL figure and reference wrong; corrected limits AD 1270-870 BC; 'probably rules out' Colonial manufacture; no use for origin. By the lab that ran the test. Paywalled.

sources.citation: Hristov, R.H. & Genovés T., S. (2001). Reply to Peter Schaaf and Günther A. Wagner's "Comments on 'Mesoamerican evidence of pre-Columbian transoceanic contacts'". Ancient Mesoamerica 12(1): 83-86.
sources.note: Abstract read: restates corrected TL limits (2870-730 BP) and addresses two objections: post-1492 import, and the head being 'planted' during excavation. Full text paywalled.

sources.citation: Huster, A.C. & Smith, M.E. (2015). A new archaeological chronology for Aztec-period Calixtlahuaca, Mexico. Latin American Antiquity 26(1): 3-25.
sources.note: Abstract read: 54 radiocarbon dates; phases Dongu AD 1130-1380, Ninupi 1380-1450, Yata 1450-1530. Does not discuss the head. Full text paywalled.

sources.citation: Smith, M.E., Borejsza, A., Huster, A. & Frederick, C.D. et al. (2013). Aztec period houses and terraces at Calixtlahuaca: the changing morphology of a Mesoamerican hilltop urban center. Journal of Field Archaeology 38(3): 227-243.
sources.note: Abstract read: Smith's team excavated at the site, occupied ca. AD 1100-1530. Background only; does not discuss the head. Full text paywalled.

sources.citation: Hristov, R.H. & Genovés T., S. (n.d., c. 2000-01). The Roman head from Tecaxic-Calixtlahuaca, Mexico: a review of the evidence. Web essay, University of New Mexico. Not peer-reviewed.
sources.note: Proponents' own web text. Passages read: 1933 find, three floors, offerings, burial 1476-1510, Boehringer, Andreae quote, MNA 'Colonial' entry, Schmidt letter, son's remark, references.

sources.citation: Hristov, R.H. & Genovés T., S. (n.d., c. 2010). The Roman head from Tecaxic-Calixtlahuaca, Mexico: a review of the evidence. Extended version of a 2001 SAA meeting paper, with a reply to M.E. Smith. Web page, University of New Mexico. Not peer-reviewed.
sources.note: Passages read: 1960 Vienna congress showing (brought by Bernal; not generally accepted), García Payón 1961 as his only lifetime text on the head, rebuttal of Smith. Undated.

sources.citation: Smith, M.E. (n.d., c. 2003; photo note Nov. 2011). The "Roman Figurine" supposedly excavated at Calixtlahuaca. Web page, Arizona State University; Internet Archive copy, 2012. Not peer-reviewed.
sources.note: Non-peer-reviewed web critique (file dated Jan 2003). Read: six alternatives, case 'weak', Paddock story, few notes, collection mix-up, possible early-Colonial offering, no Roman comparisons.

confidence_note: Provenance rests on both sides' own web texts (S6-S8), read directly but not peer-reviewed; S1-S3 read as abstracts only; the 1961 notes and Andreae's quote were not seen.
corrections: Published figure corrected: Hristov & Genovés (1999) gave a TL age of 1780 ± 400 b.p. The lab that ran the test says that figure and its reference were wrong; its limits are 870 BC-AD 1270 (S2), adopted in H&G's reply (S3).

Smith (S8) says García Payón published the head in 1960. H&G's reference lists (S6, S7) date his note to 1961, with 1960 as its showing at the Vienna Congress of Americanists. The 1961 note itself was not seen.
notes: The whole case rests on one object; H&G note that no Old World find from Mesoamerica has been accepted as proof of pre-1492 contact (S6). H&G date the burial to AD 1476-1510 but the passages read do not say how. Andreae's Severan-period attribution (c. AD 193-235) is known only as H&G quote it from Domenici 2000: 29, not located (UNVERIFIED). The draft's 'fragment of a larger figurine' detail was dropped: no source outside Wikipedia was found. H&G's two web texts differ on small details (1997 vs 1998 for their poll of senior scholars; page ranges for García Payón 1979).

open_issues: Declined moving corrections[0] to notes: it is now framed as a correction of a published figure (H&G 1999's TL age, withdrawn by the lab, S2), which the schema allows; the brief is no longer quoted.
Not added: Wagner's April 2000 letter to New Scientist (cited only by Smith, S8), not verified. H&G's rebuttal of Smith (S7) is undated, so it has no timeline entry.

Not listed as sources (unverified; no DOI/URL): García Payón 1961 (Boletín INAH 6:1-2) and Heine-Geldern 1961 (Anzeiger ÖAW phil.-hist. Kl. 98(16):117-119), known only from H&G's references. Andreae quote not located.
Dropped the draft's unattributed 'single find is a weak basis' objection (no critic named; S2 does not say it). The single-object point is now in notes.

D19 re-rating 2026-09-23: unchanged — open fits: evidence on both sides (Roman style, 1933 context account, corrected TL 870 BC-AD 1270 vs weak records, Colonial-deposition and planting doubts); none withdrawn wholesale or disproven.
